text: Crom Cruach, also Crom Croush, Cenn hostile, or Cromm Cruach, was a god of Ireland. No record of his actions survives, and yet several ancient writers set him as the supreme god of the early folk. He had, they say, a following among carved stone idols who swallowed child victims. At evSamhain, king Tigernmas offered him that homage. He killed the firstborn skulls he let fall against the haggle visage of the god, a form several link with the Killycluggan Stone whose ill face is today a display at Ireland's National Museum. Saint Patrick tore down figures of this divine kind, mirroring continent servants of faith, among them St. Martin France of Tours, who smashed hundreds of Roman and Celtic statues. Yet many rock columns, stone circles, and other revered were left whole. The place-plays of old Ireland, the Dindshenchas, tell of Crom Cruach as an image that workers. Beneath it the skulls of first-born children lay broken. So long as a third of the children were yielded to him, the fell god fed the mass with milk and-grain. His lit-idol-gold stood ringed-the-fem tight stone effigies on the field of Mag Slecht, a spot thinkers now place in northeast Cavan. Some shake hands with the Dagda, the old god whose gifts fed his sons; the scholar Vallancey said the name Crom-eocha was still but another for the Dagda.

okr.objective: Crom Cruach is the primary ancient Irish god who received child sacrifice at Samhain.
key_results: Ancient sources record Crom Cruach as the primary god of the ancient Irish.
King Tigernmas worshipped him each Samhain by sacrificing first-born children.
The Dindshenchas describes his gold idol at Mag Slecht, ringed by twelve stone figures, and St. Patrick is said to have destroyed such idols.
okr.evidence: Monaghan, Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore
